  • LaKesha Womack faced towering odds as an underfunded Democrat making her first run for public office in a North Carolina district that Donald Trump carried by 15 points two years ago.
  • Sources indicate that but as early voting surged in mid-October, she sensed she might pull off an upset over Republican Rep.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, north Carolina Rep.-elect LaKesha Womack talks to reporters Sunday at the AC Hotel in Washington as she arrives for newly introduced member orientation. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

LaKesha Womack faced towering odds as an underfunded Democrat making her first run for public office in a North Carolina district that Donald Trump carried by 15 points two years ago.

Sources indicate that but as early voting surged in mid-October, she sensed she might pull off an upset over Republican Rep. Tim Moore, the influential former speaker of the North Carolina House and a chief architect of the gerrymander that aimed to keep the 14th District safely red.

Industry observers note that “There were a lot of pins and needles,” mentioned Womack, a 49-year-old ordained minister who works at a Charlotte-based nonprofit. After seeing long lines at polling places extend into Election Day, she grew more confident: “People were ready to exercise their voice.”.

Womack – who raised less than $60,000 to Moore’s $2.1 million – eked out a 2-point win in the district, which reaches from the Charlotte suburbs to mountain counties in the west.

Recent findings suggest that saddled with an unpopular president and broad dissatisfaction with the status quo, Republican incumbents across the nation experienced a midterm drubbing last week. As of Monday evening, House Democrats had netted 42 seats, with more races left to be called. The GOP in North Carolina, a state that Trump carried three times, was among the hardest hit.

Sources indicate that democrats have so far flipped five House seats in the Tar Heel State. Besides Womack, the “blue tsunami” also swept in Paul Barringer, a lawyer who founded an outdoor clothing line, and High Point Mayor Cyril Jefferson. And Army veteran Richard Ojeda, who once served in the West Virginia Senate, defeated Rep. Richard Hudson, the chairman of the National Republican Congressional Committee.

Sources indicate that democrats also won two races that had been seen as competitive for much of the cycle. Farmer Jamie Ager flipped an open seat in the state’s mountain west, while Rep. Don Davis held on to his Eastern North Carolina district, which Republicans had redrawn in their favor.

Meanwhile, in the state’s hilly northwest corner, 11-term Republican Virginia Foxx, the chairwoman of the powerful Rules Committee, is fighting for her political future: As of Monday afternoon, former journalist Chuck Hubbard led her by 99 votes in the 5th District, though The Associated Press had yet to call the race.

Recent findings suggest that that was also true in the neighboring 10th District, where GOP incumbent Pat Harrigan had a 1-point edge over Democratic physician associate Ashley Bell. Also uncalled were a pair of contests in Eastern North Carolina, where Republican Rep. Greg Murphy clung to a 233-vote edge over Democratic former state Rep. Raymond Smith and GOP Rep. David Rouzer led Democratic social worker Kimberly Hardy by less than a point.

“Nobody could have predicted this,’’ said David Wilson Brown, who leads the Democratic Party in Gaston County near Charlotte and has lost two bids for the House, including to Foxx in 2020. “It’s a watershed moment.”.

The Democratic rout in the midterm elections was powered by victories in states with new GOP-favored maps, including Texas, Ohio and Florida.

Industry observers note that but Democrats’ success in North Carolina was especially striking given the steep structural disadvantages the party faced. Since Republicans flipped the state legislature in 2010, and with it control of the redistricting process, no House GOP incumbent had lost a general election in the Tar Heel State until last week.

This year’s  congressional map – the state's sixth in seven election cycles – was engineered by the Republican-led legislature to help the party capture 11 of the state's 14 House seats.

But the Democratic surge was so big that it easily overpowered the GOP’s built-in edge. Democratic candidates were also lifted by former Gov. Roy Cooper, whose 20-point Senate win provided the underticket with powerful coattails.

“In order for them to gerrymander our state in the way that they did, they were spread very thin,” Brown noted, referring to state Republicans. “So they were kind of ripe to be defeated that way.”.

The repeated rounds of redistricting may have also erased some of the advantages of incumbency, according to Peter L. Francia, a political science professor at East Carolina University. “If you carve up a district every two years, you've taken away some of that [advantage]. And I think that that came back and hurt Republicans in this cycle.”.

Doug Heye, a GOP strategist and a former spokesman for the Republican National Committee, said redistricting “ticked off a whole lot of voters, and really activated the Democratic base.”.

On the Republican side, voters were “less motivated because they were unexcited about Trump,’’ Heye added.

Republican incumbents accustomed to winning by comfortable margins weren’t prepared for a political environment driven by anger over the war in Iran and angst about the rising cost of living.

“Clearly, a lot of those Republicans didn’t take their elections seriously,” Heye said. “They won last time with 18 points. They weren't on anyone's radar screen, so they didn't think they had to do anything.”.

It has been revealed that womack credits her win to a grassroots campaign centered on economic complications. While her race wasn’t on the national radar – Moore, after all, won by 16 points in 2024 – and her campaign didn’t have money for ads, she was out in the district doing events every day.

In a recent development, “There are a lot of working families right now who are in the missing middle,” she said in an interview. “They make too much money to get help, but they don't make enough money to get ahead. … Someone who can be working a full-time job, but still doesn’t have enough money to buy groceries or to afford their medications or to have access to health insurance.”.

In a recent development, womack mentioned her own struggles have shaped her approach to politics. This week, she’s slated to appear in court on a felony charge for allegedly failing to return a rental car in 2019. The incident wound up in one of Moore’s attack ads.

It has been revealed that “There are so many people who [understand] what happens when you're down on your luck and you don't have enough money to make good financial decisions,’’ she said. “Most people don't want those bad decisions to be a definition of their character for the rest of their life.”.

Early in the midterm cycle, Democratic opposition research group American Bridge prepared detailed dossiers on Republican House incumbents in North Carolina.

According to recent reports, “Someone like Virginia Foxx, she’s been on the Hill forever,” said Pat Dennis, the group’s president. “She was somebody … who under the radar could be vulnerable. So we started really early.”.

American Bridge’s political arm spent $340,000 on ads targeting Foxx. One spot featured a man who identified himself as a Trump voter expressing anger at the government’s response to Hurricane Helene, which devastated the mountain communities of Western North Carolina two years ago.

Other Democrats scoffed at the group’s decision to spend money targeting entrenched Republicans far from the main House battleground.

“There was a lot of reluctance from people to really believe that that data was correct, but it was,’’ Dennis remarked. “Then over the summer, we saw her numbers collapsing, so we put paid media behind it and it really paid off.”.

Hubbard ran against Foxx two years ago and lost by almost 20 points.

Sources indicate that “I kind of had a notion I was going to do this again,’’ he said in an interview Saturday while en route to Washington for freshman orientation. “I don’t like to lose at checkers, much less a congressional race.”.

After a court-drawn map resulted in a split North Carolina delegation after the 2022 elections, state Republicans won back control of the map-making process and went on to win 10 of the state’s 14 House seats under a upcoming map two years later.

At Trump’s urging, Republicans made further tweaks to the North Carolina map last year, but the original gerrymander finally came back to bite the GOP in 2026, according to Hubbard.

“North Carolina is one of the most severely gerrymandered states,’’ he said. “And what happened was they had to steal from Peter to pay Paul. It's been referred to by political scientists as a dummymander.”.

As the vote count in the 5th District continues, Foxx, whose campaign declined to comment for this story, has requested the presence of nonpartisan election observers.

They “will serve as important, watchful eyes to ensure that this sacred process is not impeded and that all legal votes are counted in a consistent, thorough manner,’’ she posted on social media.

But even before the final races are called, Republicans are already looking to the next election.

In a recent development, heye, who expects North Carolina to remain a purple state in 2028 and beyond, cautioned the Democrats who won last week not to get too comfortable in Washington. He invoked Fred Heineman, the former Raleigh police chief who rode the 1994 “Republican Revolution” to Congress – and lasted a single term.

“Some of them will lose, and some of the people who lost may run two years from now and get their seat back,’’ he said.

One GOP operative, who requested anonymity to speak candidly, offered up a similar assessment.

Trump “didn't keep his promises” and that “just got voters very angry and suppressed the GOP base from coming out because, in a midterm election it's a base turnout contest,’’ the strategist said.

“But these Democrats are renting these districts for two years.”.

Breaking: From Practical Gifts to Wellness Moments: Holiday Trends to Watch for 2026

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2259 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Vogue

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • As the holidays beckon, a younger, fashion-led contingent of consumers across the US and Europe are upping their spend despite inflation, higher living costs and economic volatility.
  • Sources indicate that “[US consumers] are signaling that they’re going to continue to be resilient shoppers and lean into the holiday season,” indicates Brian McCarthy, Deloitte’s retail strategy leader, pinpointing millennials as the top spenders this year by a long shot — in part because of life stage.
  • Across the board, high-net-worth individuals (HNWI) are more discerning than ever — spending more where necessary, for gifts centered on individuality, performance, wellness and sentimentality.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As the holidays beckon, a younger, fashion-led contingent of consumers across the US and Europe are upping their spend despite inflation, higher living costs and economic volatility. The situation doesn’t make sense on paper, but on department store floors, the verdict is clear: The holidays are still major business for luxury — they just look a little different.

Sources indicate that “[US consumers] are signaling that they’re going to continue to be resilient shoppers and lean into the holiday season,” indicates Brian McCarthy, Deloitte’s retail strategy leader, pinpointing millennials as the top spenders this year by a long shot — in part because of life stage. “Millennials and Gen Z now have some discretionary spending, and they’re starting to hit the age where they have children,” he adds, advising that department stores focus on these two cohorts.

Across the board, high-net-worth individuals (HNWI) are more discerning than ever — spending more where necessary, for gifts centered on individuality, performance, wellness and sentimentality.

Deloitte’s holiday report predicts that average household holiday spending in the US will increase 4% year-on-year to $1,654 per household in 2026. In Europe, shoppers are expected to spend 3.4% more year-on-year this holiday season, per data from Mastercard. In the US, millennials and Gen Z will make up 50% of spending — a first since the annual study began — with both groups upping their spend at a double-digit rate year-on-year. Most holiday shoppers expect to spend the most money at either mass merchants or online, followed by department stores.

McCarthy highlights some core stats luxury retailers must consider: 72% of Gen Z say they’re interested in purchasing luxury goods as gifts for the holiday season, followed by 61% of millennials, 40% of Gen X, and 29% of baby boomers. The data also reveals that 76% of Gen Z plan on gifting clothing and accessories, up from 67% last year.

Industry observers note that the K-shaped economy — where the top end of the economy grows, but the lower end lags as inequalities widen — will ultimately benefit luxury fashion retailers, many of whom rely on the top percentile spenders to turn a profit. Nonetheless, even HNWIs are not immune to the same financial pressures as the aspirational and middle class, confirms Mintel. Analysts agree that price, value, convenience and product will dictate consumption across demographics this holiday period.

Holiday shopping at Harrods is well underway.

“Financial pressures continue to influence holiday spending, creating a resilient but resourceful consumer who is looking for deals and becoming more deliberate about where they spend,” states Brittany Steiger, Mintel’s associate principal for retail and e-commerce, noting that 72% of US luxury shoppers say price alone isn’t an indicator of luxury, and 41% consider discounts notable.

According to recent reports, the macroeconomic environment is tricky, but it’s also a well-established mood of uncertainty. Per Mintel, 59% of shoppers admit financial stress is making it harder to celebrate in the way they prefer, but 39% are still willing to spend on truly meaningful purchases. Against this backdrop, the smartest retailers have risen to the challenge, aligning their product assortments with shifting consumer trends.

Industry observers note that that stated, the rollout of Christmas shopping remains largely the same. “We typically see two distinct phases: the first is about preparation, with clients investing in their own wardrobes ahead of festive celebrations,” says Simon Longland, Harrods’s director of fashion buying, pointing to partywear, evening-wear, knitwear and exceptional outerwear. Then, “as Christmas approaches, the focus shifts toward gifting.”.

Below, Vogue Business collates this year’s key gifting predictions.

For retailers, occasion dressing continues to drive growth over the holidays, but shoppers are displaying a more playful, casual approach, tracking with a younger consumer skew.

According to recent reports, at Bloomingdale’s, ritzy festive occasionwear will be a key driver. “This holiday, we can put the pursuit of the perfect wardrobe on hold for a moment and indulge in the sheer joy of fashion for fashion’s sake,” says fashion director David Thielebeule. “After seasons of restraint, fashion is remembering how to have fun. Rich color, sumptuous textures and a little extravagance are making getting dressed feel exciting again.”.

Sebla Refiğ Devidas, Turkish retailer Communité’s chief merchandising officer, reports a similar appetite for eveningwear this holiday period. “In womenswear, we expect party dressing to be a substantial part of holiday shopping, especially pieces with interesting details that can be worn in different ways,” she claims. “There’s a sense of 1920s glamour in the lace, embellishments, fringed silk, and rich textures, reflected in pieces from Conner Ives, Dries Van Noten, Ann Demeulemeester, Simone Rocha, Anna October, Fforme and Enfants Riches Déprimés.”.

It has been revealed that at End, statement separates and directional designs from Simone Rocha, Cecilie Bahnsen, Rick Owens, Peachy Den and Gimaguas are outperforming traditional partywear. “We’re taking a broader and more fashion-led approach to occasion dressing this holiday season,” notes Martin Wieczorek, End’s chief product officer. “We’re also seeing a notable shift toward separates over dresses, with customers seeking greater versatility and long-term wardrobe value, which is reflected in our assortment”.

Recent findings suggest that within menswear, Longland notes that while established party-wear brands and tailoring services will continue to play a significant role for Harrods this holiday season, the store is already seeing clients explore more pioneering attire. “We believe menswear today is as much about individual expression as it is about the traditional codes of dressing,” he notes. “The festive season is a particularly interesting moment for this, whether clients are discovering a latest designer or investing in beautifully tailored pieces for a special occasion.”.

Even among luxury shoppers, practicality is becoming a core tenet of holiday gifting.

In a recent development, “Confidence is low and spending is still up, which tells you people are not buying less, they are buying more carefully,” reports Christophe Roberts, founder and CCO of Latest York-based concept store Seed. What’s working? “Shoes, outerwear and the good $50 gift. The one major present is getting replaced by two or three smaller [practical] ones that actually say something about you.”.

British retailer End reports an uptick in pragmatic premium outerwear gifting from brands including Our Legacy, Stone Island, Salomon, Arc’teryx, Barbour and Damson Madder. “We’re seeing menswear customers gravitate toward two key style directions,” notes Wieczorek, pointing to a continuation of outdoor dressing, functional accessories and hiking-influenced footwear. (In this vein, demand for Stone Island knits has grown 36% since October, per Lyst’s 2026 gift index.).

On the other side of menswear gifting, End also reports a hunger for relaxed tailoring and elevated outerwear — “a long tailored coat is a must!” indicates Wieczorek — from brands such as Studio Nicholson, Auralee and YMC. In keeping with this desire for lasting purchases, Mintel reports that 71% of US men see luxury purchases as a personal milestone or marker of achievement, which makes meaningful wardrobe upgrades and keepsake gifts especially resonant. “We’re seeing strong momentum across jewellery and watches, a category that continues to gain traction during the gifting season as customers seek elevated, personal, enduring purchases,” says Wieczorek.

Calvin Klein underwear remains a strong stocking filler, boosted by the brand’s hit campaign.

In Newly introduced York-based concept store Essx, utility reigns supreme among menswear shoppers, bolstered by more experimental outerwear. “As the holiday season approaches, we expect to see a continued focus on utility shopping paired with experimental and statement outerwear. Leather has been one of our strongest categories over the past few seasons with VIPs and walk-in clients,” notes Jackson Ray, store director. “We anticipate a continued desire for leather pants and jackets paired with sterling silver accessories and leather boots.”.

Sources indicate that essx also predicts keepsake pieces to perform. “Our customers always seek exclusive or limited items,” says Ray. “We have heavily invested in upscale accessories such as fine jewelry, eyewear, and footwear, which make for fantastic holiday gifts.

Sources indicate that unsurprisingly, underwear remains a trusty stocking filler for shoppers, especially this time round. Demand for men’s Calvin Klein underwear climbed 60% year-on-year in October 2026 versus October 2025, according to Lyst’s 2026 gift index. Following the Jude Bellingham campaign, searches soared a further 25% week-on-week (Nov 2-9 2026).

According to recent reports, womenswear shoppers are also seeking timeless gifts this holiday season. “For womenswear, quality, versatility and longevity can help justify the splurge,” says Steiger, noting that 76% of US luxury consumers prefer timeless or classic styles, where pieces feel special enough to gift but relevant beyond the holiday season. At Selfridges, HNWIs are showing strong interest in labels such as Phoebe Philo and The Row for this holiday season. “Investment dressing continues to be a key theme, with elevated knitwear emerging as a standout category,” notes Bosse Myhr, director of buying for menswear, womenswear and childrenswear at Selfridges.

Retailers still want to see newness within established brands, though. “This Christmas marks an key moment for womenswear at Harrods, as many of the collections introduced by newly appointed creative directors began arriving in store for SS26,” explains Longland. “These upcoming creative visions are bringing fresh energy to established houses, and we expect the new icons emerging from these collections to feature prominently on Christmas wish lists.” Longland notes that Harrods’s clients are responding to pieces that feel distinctive, rather than plainly familiar.

Tried-and-tested holiday favorites will remain core across genders. “In our stores right now, we’ve rolled out cashmere shops, scarf bars, trench destinations and gifting at all levels of luxury prices,” noted Burberry CEO Joshua Schulman, on the brand’s latest earnings call. Burberry just staged a takeover of New York hotel The Mark to promote its scarves and partywear with the all-important US consumer. Flannels features the Burberry scarf bars in-store, too. “You can’t go wrong with an iconic British scarf for Christmas. It’s one of those gifts that feels special but will be worn for years to come,” says Natalie Dickson, Frasers Group’s head of luxury brand partnerships.

In a recent development, according to PWC, 78% of US Gen Z consumers are seeking nostalgic, screen-free gifts. For US consumers gifting children (17 and under) in their family, clothing and footwear were the second most-cited category (60%), following toys (63%). Each of the top five categories are all analog.

Recent findings suggest that in line with Gen Z and millennial households stepping into parenthood — and therefore becoming core gift-givers — childrenswear is showing more and more affinities with adult tastes. “There’s a growing crossover between adult and childrenswear, with families shopping the designer brands they know and love across the whole family,” reports Dickson.

According to recent reports, at Harrods, a similar shift holds, with childrenswear holiday demand led by the same categories driving womenswear and menswear: partywear, pyjamas and outerwear. “Christmas at Harrods is one of those moments when dressing becomes a shared family occasion,” says Longland. “From special outfits for celebrations to beautiful winter pieces, clients are looking for clothing that combines practicality with a sense of occasion.”.

The new Burberry Christmas campaign.

One of the most notable areas of growth within childrenswear has been the baby category, which has significantly outperformed the broader children’s market at Selfridges this year, notes Myhr.

Sources indicate that in the kids category, parents’ own memories of Christmas and holiday style guide product assortments. “There’s a wonderful nostalgia to dressing children for the holidays, and nobody understands that quite like Ralph Lauren,” says Bloomingdale’s Thielebeule, calling out Fair Isle knits, tartan and velvet. For him, these are tropes that “feel as though they belong in today’s family holiday card, but are just as lovely a generation later.”.

Last year, Ralph Lauren’s big Christmas push went viral. In response, Bloomingdale’s has invested in a special holiday partnership this year, entitled “A Treasured World”, which offers a whole family range of gifting and cozy seasonal wear, explains Thielebeule. It builds on the viral traction Ralph Lauren demonstrated last year with “Ralph Lauren Mom” creators on TikTok and Instagram presenting themselves as festive, old-money Americans, he adds.

In a recent development, luxury brands have been ramping up their investments in wellness this holiday season — tapping into a market now valued at $2.7 trillion, according to McKinsey. This has trickled down into holiday offerings. “Wellness is opening latest territory for luxury gifting, particularly as consumers increasingly invest in how they feel as well as how they look,” says Mintel’s Steiger, citing Dior’s “Haute Wellness” capsule, rolled out in September, which comprises a Pilates and yoga mat, a yoga block, a Pilates ring, resistance bands and weighted wristbands.

According to recent reports, in self-gifting, 32% of US shoppers cited health and wellness products as tempting — making them the third-highest-scoring category in Deloitte’s survey, after clothing and accessories, and electronics. Meanwhile, 44% of shoppers will gift products from the health and wellness category this year, up from 40% in 2025. Fittingly, one of the top brands in Lyst’s gifting index is Alo, with demand increasing 132% this year.

The rise in wellness gifting aligns with another undercurrent. Per PWC, 81% of US Gen Z consumers are prioritizing offline, in-person activities this year, with 63% saying a shared meal would matter more as a gift than a physical present.

Nonetheless, the bottom line remains the same across gift categories. “This holiday, the opportunity is in products that offer something beyond the price tag, whether that’s emotional significance, lasting quality, personal wellbeing, or simply something worth keeping,” claims Steiger.

Bourbon Caramel Apple Pie

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways

  • Welcome to Bon Appétit Bake Club, a community of curious bakers.
  • 2 hours 15 minutes (plus 7 hours for chilling and cooling).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that the one thing that can make classic apple pie better? Caramel! That it’s laced with a generous dose of bourbon vaults it straight into hall-of-fame territory. Made using a double batch of our never-fail Perfect Pie Crust, this pretty lattice-topped pie is a crowd-pleaser, familiar enough to appeal to the traditionalists with just enough of a surprise from the booze and the smoky burnt sugar to make the thrill-seekers come back for more. Like all good things, apple pie can’t be rushed. It needs time to chill, bake, and rest—so blueprint ahead, especially if it’s for Thanksgiving.

Welcome to Bon Appétit Bake Club, a community of curious bakers. Each month senior Test Kitchen editors Jesse Szewczyk and Shilpa Uskokovic share a must-make recipe and dive deep on why it works. Come bake and learn with us—ask questions, share pics, listen to our podcast, and lots more here. And don't forget to join the Bake Club Group chat over on Substack.

2 hours 15 minutes (plus 7 hours for chilling and cooling).

In a recent development, whisk 3⅓ cups (417 g) all-purpose flour, 2 tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and ½ tsp. baking powder in a large bowl to combine. Add 4 oz. chilled cream cheese, cut into 1" pieces; rub into dry ingredients with your fingers until incorporated (mixture will look very shaggy). Add 1¼ cups (2½ sticks) chilled unsalted butter, sliced ½" thick, and toss to coat in flour, then smash with your fingers into smaller, flatter pieces (about chickpea-size).

Industry observers note that make a well in the center of mixture and pour in ½ cup ice water. Toss with a fork or your hands to distribute, then knead in bowl a couple of times to bring dough together (some dry bits may remain).

Sources indicate that turn out dough onto a surface lightly dusted with rice flour or all-purpose flour; dust top of dough with flour. Roll out to a ½"-thick rectangle. Fold dough in half, rotate 90°, and fold in half again. Roll out again to a ½"-thick rectangle and repeat folding process, dusting with more flour as needed to prevent sticking. Divide dough in half and pat each piece into a ½"-thick disk. Wrap each disk tightly in plastic. Chill at least 2 hours and, preferably, up to 12 hours.

According to recent reports, do Ahead: Dough can be made 1 month ahead. Wrap each disk in 2 layers of plastic and freeze instead of chilling. Thaw in refrigerator 12 hours before using.

Place 1 cup (200 g) granulated sugar and ½ cup water in a medium Dutch oven or other heavy pot and cover. Bring to a boil over medium heat (no need to stir); cook until sugar is dissolved, 4–7 minutes total. Uncover and continue to cook, stirring or swirling pot occasionally, until caramel turns a deep golden brown, 10–12 minutes.

Add zest of 1 lemon, 3 lb. Honeycrisp apples (about 6 large), peeled, cored, quartered, thinly sliced crosswise, ½ cup bourbon, 4 Tbsp. unsalted butter, 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and 1 tsp. ground cinnamon to caramel (it may become stiff). Cover and cook, stirring occasionally, until caramel dissolves and apples have released a generous amount of liquid and are tender but still retain their shape (they should look mostly translucent), 15–18 minutes.

Stir ⅓ cup heavy cream, 3 Tbsp. cornstarch, and 2 Tbsp. cool water in a small bowl until cornstarch is dissolved. Pour into apple mixture and cook (it should be bubbling), stirring often, until mixture is thick, about 5 minutes. Transfer filling to a large bowl; let cool. Cover and chill until cold, at least 45 minutes.

Sources indicate that meanwhile, let dough sit at room temperature 5 minutes. Unwrap 1 disk and roll out on a surface lightly dusted with rice flour or all-purpose flour to a 12" round, about ¼" thick. Brush excess flour from dough and wrap around rolling pin. Transfer to a 9"-diameter pie pan (such as East Fork Spun Iron Pie Dish). Unfurl into pan, then lift edges and allow dough to slump down into pan. Trim, leaving about a 1" overhang. Chill 15 minutes.

Unwrap remaining disk; roll out on surface lightly dusted with more rice flour to a 18x12" rectangle, about ⅛" thick. Brush excess flour from dough and transfer to a large parchment-lined baking sheet. Brush dough with a thin film of cold water; sprinkle remaining ¼ cup (50 g) granulated sugar over and press gently with your hands to cover dough completely in an even layer (coating dough before cutting into strips will give you the most even coverage). Chill 15 minutes.

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 375°. Spoon chilled filling into pie pan and smooth surface to level. Using a ruler, cut dough rectangle into 1"-wide strips. Lay 5–8 strips over filling, spacing evenly across surface to cover. Weave another 5–8 strips over, then under, alternating to create a lattice crust (you may not use all of the strips). Trim overhang to match bottom crust. Press edges of top and bottom crusts firmly together to seal, then trim again, leaving about ¼" overhang. Fold overhang up and over lattice so crust is flush with edges of pan and crimp as desired with lightly floured fingers.

Place pan on a rimmed baking sheet (to catch drips) and bake pie until crust is set and golden, 45–50 minutes. Reduce oven temperature to 350°; continue to bake until crust is deep golden brown and filling is bubbling up through lattice, 40–50 minutes more. Transfer pan to a wire rack and let pie cool in pan at least 4 hours before serving.

It has been revealed that do Ahead: Filling can be made 2 days ahead; keep chilled. Pie can be baked 1 day ahead; store, loosely covered, at room temperature.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that for some people there isn’t much of a debate around who makes the best cast-iron skillet. There is a die-hard fan base loyal to the affordable US-made Lodge cast-iron pan that will not hear of any other suggestions.

There are others (cast-iron nerds and collectors) who swear by the superior quality of their vintage pan from Griswold or Wagner that they found at a scrap yard, de-rusted in a bucket with a DIY electrolysis setup, and seasoned with a proprietary oil blend in the furnaces of their bespoke restoration workshop.

According to recent reports, to these two camps of people I say: “I don’t want to fight you, and I already know why you feel the way you feel. Please do not send me any angry emails.”.

Sources indicate that if you’ve been loyal to your own cast-iron pan for years—or decades—I don’t expect to change your mind. My goal is merely to provide recommendations for cast-iron cookware based on side-by-side testing and the input collectively provided by members of our staff. Agree with me and my team or don’t; either way, I’m happy if people are passionate about cooking with cast iron because I too enjoy it a great deal.

Industry observers note that cast-iron frying pans were the original nonstick pans, before ceramic nonstick and PTFE rolled around, and unlike modern nonstick coatings, a cast-iron pan’s surface actually gets more nonstick over time rather than degrading week by week. This is because, through continued cooking, thin layers of oil polymerize to the surface of the pan, creating a glassy nonstick surface that improves with continued use. They are also strong enough to handle metal utensils. The same can’t be noted for that Instagram-famous nonstick pan (you know the one).

Yes, there are ways you can damage this seasoning layer, but these pans are far more resilient than lots of people think, and they aren’t actually all that difficult to care for. Talk to cast-iron enthusiasts and they’ll tell you the best way to season a cast-iron skillet is to just keep cooking with it.

Industry observers note that and cook with it you can. Cast-iron pans are amazing for fried eggs, skillet hashes, cornbread, and sautéed greens. At a high heat, they do an incredible job searing strip steaks, London broil, and chicken thighs, giving you a burnished crispy exterior.

Bottom line, cast-iron cooking is an absolute joy, and every kitchen tool kit should include some cast iron alongside its stainless-steel and carbon steel pans and enameled Dutch oven.

Fresh in this enhancement: A review of Made In's new cast-iron pan as well as more long-term testing information for our winner.

Size(s): 10.5" (4.5 lb.), 12" (6 lb.), 13.5" (7.5 lb.)Pre-seasoned: Yes.

In a recent development, what I loved: Because they’re much more expensive than the Lodges folks got used to, many feel a certain type of way about the newly introduced era of smooth, vintage-style cast-iron pans that includes this Lancaster. But when you have the opportunity to test a bunch of these pans side by side, you really get a sense of their differences (however small), and you’d be surprised by the things you notice. It was in this apples-to-apples testing that this pan, manufactured by a small tech giant based in Southeastern Pennsylvania, really set itself apart.

Industry observers note that the Lancaster is the lightest cast-iron pan I’ve tested, weighing in at 4 lb. for the No. 8 (10"-diameter) pan. Most cast-iron pans of a similar size are around 5 lb. or more—a seemingly small difference in number that makes a surprisingly big difference in hand. When laid out next to a dozen pans in the Test Kitchen, multiple testers singled out this pan as being the most comfortable to hold and maneuver.

It has thinner walls than a typical cast-iron skillet, which allows it to heat up faster. In testing, it came to temp over one minute faster than pans with thicker walls. We were concerned this would mean a reduction in the level of heat retention you’d want to crisp up the edges of some skillet cornbread, but we didn’t find that to be a problem at all. The cooking surface also demonstrated relatively even heat for a cast-iron pan (you really can’t expect too much from cast iron, though; cold spots are sort of inevitable with the material).

The pan comes pre-seasoned, but as is the case with most smooth cast-iron pans, this seasoning layer isn’t nearly as robust as what you’d find on a conventional Lodge or Victoria pan. The polished surface does aid in the pan’s nonstick properties, though, so we found the pan was exceptionally nonstick right out of the box.

In a recent development, other testing sites have criticized this style of smooth cast-iron pan for getting stained after cooking, but to that we say: This is the process of seasoning developing on the pan. That staining is a feature, not a bug.

An earlier design of this pan didn’t include a helper handle, a feature we missed but forgave because the pan was already so easy to wield. However, Lancaster recently updated the design to include one—all the better in our book. Check out my full review of the Lancaster No. 8 here.

What I’d leave: The main drawback here is the cost. This pan will set you back $175, a steep price for cookware with a reputation for being budget-friendly. I’ll just say this: People happily pay comparable prices for nonstick ceramic cookware that lasts only a year or two at best. This pan, provided you don’t drop it in an industrial crucible, will last a lifetime.

It has been revealed that in the long run: I have more patience than a lot of people when it comes to taking care of pans. So I will concede that the out of the box seasoning isn’t that robust. Some tasks, like searing off meat, can strip the seasoning slightly at first. With the Lancaster, I’ve found that this doesn’t impact the pans overall nonstick-ness. It does, however, mean you have to keep an eye out for rust until it gets a couple uses under its belt.

In a recent development, below you’ll see two Lancaster pans. The left is four years old and the right is fresh from the box (you can tell because the earlier generation of pans didn’t have the helper handle). These are the pans after searing off two chicken thighs. You can see how the pan on the left has a robust, established seasoning, while the one on the right has some gray patches where the chicken skin pulled off some of that seasoning. From experience (I am the owner of the pan on the left), I can say that all you really need to do is keep cooking with it to get that seasoning back, but if you want to do a whole round of seasoning in the oven yourself, it certainly won’t hurt. Honestly, had I just sautéed some onions in the rendered schmaltz after cooking the chicken, those spots would be taken care of.

For comparison, I seared some chicken thighs in both pans. The factory seasoning might get patchy after the first use. Don’t let that scare you, just keep cooking with it. If you’re really worried about rust, just wipe down the surface of the pan with a tiny bit of neutral oil, buff off the excess, and put it over the heat for a few minutes.

Industry observers note that some people complain about the cosmetic changes to these smooth pans when breaking them in To reiterate: It does not impact the performance of the pan. If it bothers you, I encourage you to think about how it’s a record of use and proof that it’s growing and developing alongside you. Or, if you’re just an unsentimental aesthete, perhaps read up on the concept of wabi-sabi. I personally think that my pan is the most beautiful piece of cookware I own!

In a recent development, if you want a high-quality pan that’s not only a pleasure to cook with, but can serve as a family heirloom for generations to come, consider this one. If you’re just looking for a workhorse that won’t break the bank, go for the budget option below.

Size(s): 4.8" (1.1 lb.), 6.5" (2 lb.), 8" (3.1 lb.), 10" (5.5 lb.), 12" (7.5 lb.)Pre-seasoned: Yes.

What I loved: Again, I apologize for snubbing Lodge, as even in our office we have a number of staunch brand loyalists. But in my testing, the Victoria edged out the fan favorite on two separate metrics. Victoria pans are pre-seasoned with flaxseed oil and arrive glossy and exceptionally nonstick. Having a more thorough pre-seasoning is more crucial on cast-iron pans, as they are prone to sticking early on. We found the Victoria pan’s factory seasoning slicker than Lodge’s, which made frying potatoes and eggs ever so slightly easier. Do all cast-iron seasonings improve with continued use over time? Yes. But we know that some people want as much of a head start as they can get, and this pan offers you the best one.

According to recent reports, the other way the Victoria bested the Lodge is in its form factor. The pour spouts on the Victoria are nice and wide, making it easy to pour off oil or other pan juices, and testers found the handle shape slightly more comfortable than the Lodge.

I’ll be honest, though, these differences are pretty small, and if you feel drawn to the Lodge name, I recommend it as well.

Sources indicate that what I’d leave: Given it’s bargain pricing, there isn’t much to dislike here. I will note this pan is significantly heavier than the Lancaster pan—a full pound and a half for the same diameter skillet. Heavier skillets are cheaper and easier to produce, so it’s a trade-off you’ll have to accept if you want a less expensive piece of cookware.

Recent findings suggest that 1. We had several members of staff handle the pans to get a broad sense of how easy the pans were to maneuver. Then we got to cooking.

It has been revealed that 2. Using a little bit of oil, we fried eggs sunny-side up and scrambled to see how much (if anything) stuck to the pan.

3. We seared skin-on chicken thighs to get a sense of how evenly heat was distributed around the cooking surface. We also measured how long it took for the pan to reach 375° at medium heat.

4. We washed the pans in hot water, noting any places where seasoning might have worn away.

According to recent reports, 5. We re-seasoned the pans ourselves in an oven for an hour at 500°.

It has been revealed that 6. We cooked another round of eggs to observe any changes.

In a recent development, I omitted enameled cast-iron skillets like those made by Le Creuset or Staub because enameled surfaces offer a different experience in terms of both cooking and care. I also chose to exclude any cast-iron griddles or grill pans since they are too different functionally.

It has been revealed that sizing is a bit different from company to company, but I chose to stick with a 10"-diameter skillet—a No. 8 in traditional cast-iron sizing—as it is the most common size available.

How nonstick is the pan out of the box?

I should clarify that cast-iron pans aren’t nonstick in the sense that you can cook an egg in the pan without any oil and slide it around. A really well-seasoned pan that’s a glossy lacquered black from years of use might get close, but the seasoning really just helps food release more easily from the pan—and the more seasoning there is, the less oil you’ll need for food to release.

I evaluated the pans on their out-of-the-box factory seasoning, because having a solid seasoning layer to start with diminishes the amount of time you need to break in a pan. This matters more with cheaper, rough textured cast iron, which is more prone to sticking when it lacks proper seasoning. For polished or vintage-style cast-iron pans (like the Lancaster), factory seasoning is nice, but the smooth surface also aids in preventing sticking, so it isn’t as crucial in the beginning stages of using the pan. That is why, throughout this review you see more emphasis on factory seasoning when discussing budget pans.

Is the pan designed in a way that makes it easy to use?

I counted form and design heavily in how I judged these pans. I wanted the pan to be comfortable and easy to maneuver, so I looked for pans that were lightweight (relatively, we’re talking about iron here) and had handles that were comfortable to grip. If the pan was heavier, I wanted a helper handle for moving it from the cooktop to the oven. I didn’t place an emphasis on whether handle was designed to stay cool, because even a handle billed as “stay cool” will get dangerously hot when cooking for long enough, so I feel it’s better to just make a habit of always using an oven mitt or cloth to grab a cast-iron handle.

According to recent reports, heavy-duty, even-heating, satisfyingly weighty skillets are staples in the BA Test Kitchen because of their versatility. Stainless-steel and carbon steel frying pans get hot quickly, but they don’t always have the heat-retention capabilities of cast iron. And while nonstick pans are nice for scrambled eggs and crispy-skinned fish, many are not oven-safe and should never be exposed to high temperatures, so you can’t sear safely with them.

Stargazer Cast Iron Skillet - 10.5".

The Stargazer is a lovely pan. Like the Lancaster, its a vintage-style skillet, so it has a smooth texture that’s easy to clean. The surface develops seasoning well, and the curved lip allows for easy pouring at any angle. Ultimately, it is one of the heavier high-end skillets available on the market, which is why we don’t have it as a winner. However, if weight isn’t a huge concern for you, it is still an excellent pan.

Sources indicate that if you know cast-iron pans, you might see the Yeti cast-iron skillet and might find that it looks somewhat familiar. This is because Yeti acquired cult-favorite Butter Pat several years ago. The Yeti skillet is just the Butter Pat by a upcoming name, and apart from the logo, the finish, handle shape, and overall design remain unchanged. This pan has a nice velvety surface that holds on to seasoning very well, while still maintaining a smooth, glossier finish that makes vintage-style pans so desirable. Small gripes: The handle design wasn’t a favorite among testers, and the side walls are a slightly shorter than most other cast-iron pans. It’s also a touch heavier and a couple touches more expensive than our winner. Still, this is an excellent cast-iron pan and makes a great family heirloom.

Lodge Cast-Iron Skillet with Red Mini Silicone Hot Handle Holder, 8".

People who track recommendations like these tend to be shocked that we don’t place the Lodge as our winner or budget pick. It is a fantastic pan, make no mistake. It has a great factory seasoning that’s resilient from the jump, and the 10" costs around twenty bucks—so what gives? When it came down to it, the Victoria pan had a slicker factory seasoning out of the box and a more comfortable handle design.

It has been revealed that smithey No. 10 Cast-Iron Skillet.

Another high-end polished cast-iron pan on the list. Smithey pans are gorgeous, so much so that it almost feels wrong cooking with them. However, you should cook with it straight away, as the factory seasoning is a little light on these, and we observed a little bit wearing away after the first couple rounds of cooking prior to us adding an additional layer of seasoning. Senior editor Noah Kaufman has been cooking with the Smithey multiple times a week for a couple years and claims that within a few months of regular use and two bouts of seasoning in the oven he no longer worried about stuck eggs or steaks.

Recent findings suggest that gorgeous as they are, Smithey pans are heavy, though, at 5.8 lb. for the 10" skillet.

This skillet is the second lightest (4.3 lb. at 10") and has a velvety surface that holds on to seasoning a little better than the smooth polished pans. Like the Stargazer, it also has a curved lip instead of a pour spout, but I found that this pan does have a bit of a dribbling problem, which I wasn't crazy about. Still, one member of our team who has now lived with this pan for years loves it and uses it every day.

Lodge Cast-Iron Blacklock Skillet, Triple Seasoned - 10.25".

Lodge released this pan in response to the wave of newly introduced and fancy polished pans, and as beautiful (quite beautiful), well-seasoned (three glossy layers), and lightweight as it is (almost even with the Lancaster), our testers found the handle uncomfortable to hold.

Ooni is a pizza oven company, and this pan is really designed for cooking in an oven rather than on the stovetop. It has a detachable handle, which is actually a genius bit of design that makes it easy and comfortable to grab out of a blazing hot pizza oven. But the sides are too shallow for doing more normal cast-iron things like frying chicken or sautéing greens. It is, however, great for cornbread and pizookies.

This is Made In’s official entry into the cast-iron newly introduced wave. The pan has a smooth machined surface, nice design touches, like curved sidewalls and a spacious helper handle. The primary handle is nice to hold; however, a longer handle can make a pan feel heavier and add strain on the wrists. This pan is not the lightest, either. I found it difficult to transport the full pan from the stovetop to the oven using only one hand, so consider this a pan for people with meaty forearms. Made In also uses flaxseed oil for the factory seasoning, which is a controversial choice in the cast-iron world. The reason for that controversy is that, while the finish flaxseed oil produces is glossy and attractive, it tends to be brittle. Especially with newer pans, a flaxseed seasoning has a tendency to wear away with regular cooking. After testing, I did notice this pan had some gray (unseasoned) patches after a round of searing meat. Again, not a big deal—just keep cooking with it— but something to keep in mind. All of that being noted, I do still think this is a high-quality pan. During the cooking tests, I had absolutely no complications with sticking whatsoever.

Recent findings suggest that this pan is pretty similar to a standard Lodge or Victoria, but with a seasoning that’s not as nonstick out of the box. We did find, however, that it added latest layers of seasoning quite well.

Valor Pre-seasoned Cast-Iron Skillet.

The Valor is apparently a favorite in restaurants, but there’s nothing special to it that makes it stand out. If anything, the pour spouts are so small they might as well not be there at all.

According to recent reports, we’re all for innovation, which is what Finex sought to do with its octagonal pan and its bulbous handle, but we didn’t really observe any value from the modifications. While the octagonal shape is easier for flipping you could just use a bigger cast-iron pan for anything you want to flip. And its “speed cool” handle was awkward to hold.

Recent findings suggest that anytime KitchenAid ventures beyond the small appliance space you never quite know what you’re gonna get. In this case, it’s a cast-iron pan that is totally average in every way, except for its minimalist modern design. We think this pan is too expensive for what you’re getting.

In a recent development, “Ooh, a lid!” Was the universal reaction to this cast-iron pan. If you like the idea of having a lid for your pan, then this is your pan. The problem with cast-iron lids, though, is that they don’t benefit from the progressive seasoning development the rest of the pan gets as you cook with it. Lids are only really dealing with evaporative moisture, which makes them even more likely to rust. Smithey, up above, sells glass lids that fit their pans, which, while not as oven-safe, won’t have that rust problem.

This is Victoria’s answer to the high-end polished cast-iron pan. The seasoning is great, but the pan is heavier than the Lancaster, and we didn’t love all the extra design embellishments. The brass insert on the handle had no practical value (it heated up quicker than the surrounding cast iron). Also, all the extra ridges and divots just meant more places for gunk to get stuck in.

Amazon customers really like this pan. It comes with a silicone handle cover and a glass lid, which is nice (glass is a better material for a lid than cast iron). It also has tall 3" sides that make this pan great for frying. Beyond that, though, the pan is heavy and seemed to be barely pre-seasoned.

Industry observers note that this is a super polished cast-iron pan with a glossy cooking surface that was nice to work with. However, we noticed quite a few cosmetic problems, like small nicks and rough edges that made it seem like there were some corners cut in the manufacturing process.

Another pan that is just fine. The factory seasoning is minimal, so you’ll have to build that up yourself. There are several better options that are just as affordable from Victoria, Lodge, and others.

This is an affordable pan that looks a lot like a Lodge, but with a lesser factory seasoning.

Amazon Basics Pre-seasoned Cast-Iron Pan.

Recent findings suggest that the seasoning that came on this pan out of the box was pretty bad, and with so many other cheap alternatives that offer much better quality, we don’t see the point in purchasing this pan. It’s also only available in a 15" diameter at the time of writing, which is bigger (and heavier) than most people need.

Recent findings suggest that when you first get your pan, you’ll want to season it. We recommend this even when the pan comes labeled as pre-seasoned. To do this, just lightly rub a bone-dry pan with a thin layer of high-heat neutral vegetable oil and place it upside down in a very hot oven—450°F–500°F should do the trick. Leave for an hour, turn off the heat, let it cool completely in the oven (you should be able to take it out without an oven mitt or towel), rub with a tiny bit more oil, and store. You can season cast iron as many times as you’d like to build up a glossy nonstick surface; when the pan looks dull or dry, it’s time to moisturize.

No, you can’t chuck it in the dishwasher, and you won’t be using your normal hand-wash methods, but a cast-iron skillet really doesn’t require much love. When it’s time to clean up, simply wipe a damp rag across the surface of your pan, then dry it thoroughly. Often, that’ll be enough. But if there are any crusty bits, try pouring coarse salt in there and going at it with a Tawashi scrubber, which has soft bristles that whisk away any detritus. Many will tell you to avoid soap at all costs lest you ruin your careful seasoning, but a little dish soap is fine—just don’t let it sit in hot water. (Read our complete guide to cleaning cast iron.).

Industry observers note that for really baked on crumbs, try The Ringer, a handy chain mail scrubber that easily rinses clean between uses. After cleaning your cast iron, be sure to wipe your fry pan very dry—this is key for preventing any rust spots. Then take a teeny bit of neutral cooking oil (like canola or vegetable), smear on a paper towel, and give it a light coating. Take care to get the handle and the bottom as well as the cooking surface, as rust can crop up anywhere. And you’re good to go! It sounds involved, but it really only takes a few minutes. A well-seasoned pan takes virtually no time at all, so dutifully season and you’ll be rewarded.

Tossed your skillet in the sink absentmindedly or left it out in the rain only to find it’s developed a layer of orange rust? Don’t panic—rusting can happen pretty easily if you allow your pan to come into contact with water for an extended period of time (it is made of iron, after all). But that doesn’t mean it’s ruined. A salt scrub will help with most small spots, while a vinegar soak is the cure for more serious cases. (Read more on dealing with pesky cast-iron rust patches.).

Recent findings suggest that if, after all of that, you’re still intimidated by raw cast-iron cookware, you might want to consider an enameled cast-iron skillet. It offers all of the heat retention and distribution of a well-seasoned cast-iron pan, plus it has a porcelain enamel to prevent rusting. Unlike a Le Creuset Dutch oven, enameled cast-iron skillets, like Staub’s, have a dark textured enamel that helps with browning and crisping.

Sources indicate that wilder Davies: I have been Epicurious and Bon Appétit’s resident cookware tester and researcher for over six years. I have cooked with hundreds and hundreds of pans and have asked chefs, materials scientists, and manufacturers far too many questions about things that go clank in the kitchen. I am a major apologist of nonstick alternatives, and strongly believe in a buy-it-for-life ethos when it comes to outfitting your pantry.

#7766. Is Merch Stealing Luxury’s Aspirational Consumer?

Is Merch Stealing Luxury’s Aspirational Consumer?

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1506 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Vogue

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Typically, middle-income young shoppers have focused their fashion spending on accessible luxury goods or one-off splurges, like a Coach Tabby bag ($375) or a Longchamp Le Pliage ($165).
  • However, among these groups, a growing faction is trading down, looking instead to the fast-developing category of merch to broadcast their affiliation to culture, whether it’s the newly introduced Rhode windbreaker ($257) or last week’s frenzied release of a hot-pink GTA logo tee ($66).
  • “Brands invest inordinate amounts of resources into product research and development to try and catch the ever-elusive hype cycle.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Typically, middle-income young shoppers have focused their fashion spending on accessible luxury goods or one-off splurges, like a Coach Tabby bag ($375) or a Longchamp Le Pliage ($165).

However, among these groups, a growing faction is trading down, looking instead to the fast-developing category of merch to broadcast their affiliation to culture, whether it’s the newly introduced Rhode windbreaker ($257) or last week’s frenzied release of a hot-pink GTA logo tee ($66). While merch is nothing fresh in the fashion market — Balenciaga relied heavily on it during Demna’s tenure between 2015 and 2025 — the playing field is changing, with a stronger focus on the temporal buzz of a new digital or game-based craze, the cult movie everyone’s watching, the fiendishly anticipated alt-rap tour, or a new milestone in a girl-boss beauty community’s trajectory — like Rhode founder Hailey Bieber’s 30th birthday.

“Brands invest inordinate amounts of resources into product research and development to try and catch the ever-elusive hype cycle. But with [consumers] suddenly coveting more transient ‘merchandise’ over main line product ranges, is that investment misplaced?” asks Simon Richardson, group strategy director at creative agency Amplify. “What [brands] should be doing is creating a moment in time, not just a product line. Fans need more — all the time — to signal what they care about in a way that feels distinct, real and truly of a moment.”.

Outside the Selfridges GTA launch.

Sources indicate that recently, Jordan Firstman, director of buzzy gay drama Club Kid, called on Latest York designer Emily Dawn Long — renowned among Dimes Square it-kids for her in-the-know screenprinted vintage tees — to design the merch for the film. The designer, known for her Spoiled Boys slogan tee, emblazoned the ragged tops with one of the film’s lines, “It’s like that every time”. In the film itself, Firstman also wore his own Emily Dawn Long tee, printed with the words, “Take off your clothes”. On Wednesday, A24 took over a downtown 1<3 NY souvenir shop to sell the capsule, before releasing a limited online drop (most styles are sold out).

A24 worked with designer Emily Dawn Long for upcoming film Club Kid’s merch.

Tech bros are also tapping in. This year, Trump-contracted data surveillance firm Palantir released a chore jacket ($239) not dissimilar to those purveyed by cult restaurants, such as Sessions Arts Club and St. John. Reportedly, the company’s broader apparel line is performing, especially in South Korea, where the windbreaker ($170) sold out. Much-talked-about corporation Nvidia — whose CEO Jensen Huang stepped down this week following his extramarital affair with a potential Chinese spy — also released a sweater emblazoned with a leather-jacketed cartoon of Huang ($178). The design is picking up strong resale value again following the scandal: one seller listed the design on Ebay for $2,500. And OpenAI offers a racing-style shirt ($75) not dissimilar to styles from Corteiz, Palace and Supreme — as well as bumper stickers ($10) and caps ($40), all sold on its website.

Recent findings suggest that as luxury struggles to justify its price hikes — since the average price of personal luxury goods increased by 52% between 2019 and 2024, per HSBC — the merch market has swooped in to capitalize on the aspirational shopper. In the US, consumer sentiment is low, and yet spending is up. Indeed, across the US, Europe and China, shoppers are more cautious and discerning with discretionary purchases, guided by a brand’s value propositions. If a band tee, a Roblox hoodie, or a pair of GTA x Travis Scott Nike Air Force 1 sneakers can communicate cultural belonging, community adjacency, and lifestyle for a fraction of the cost of a luxury handbag, then merch wins.

It has been revealed that indeed, in late 2025, 72% of Gen Z luxury shoppers told Vogue Business they would prefer owning a Walmart “Wirkin” over a genuine Hermès Birkin, and when interviewed, several respondents mentioned they deem spending lots of money on luxury distasteful and that luxury goods are not worth the cost. At the same time, beauty continues to boom with aspirational shoppers, but — unlike clothing and accessories — has only a handful of ways to turn its goods into walking advertisements. The Rhode phone case, seen in influencer selfies, marked the first step towards a solution, then came the wearable merch. Similarly, tech giants largely deal in intangible goods. But physical merch is a way for fans to display their favorite chip-maker or AI platform.

Hailey Bieber wears her upcoming Rhode windbreaker, which retails at $257.

For beauty, and even tech, merch gives brand fans a way to express their appreciation of the products and the communities around them. Companies recognize young people’s appetite to feel part of something.

According to recent reports, millennial readers will remember when “merch” referred primarily to band T-shirts. That playbook began in musical subcultures and has now transferred to a broader market. “Gen Alpha grew up inside worlds. For them, a ‘skin’ [Fortnite’s in-game outfits] is merch, a creator’s snack bar is merch, and a hoodie is the physical version of a world they already spend hours in,” claims Jolyon Varley, co-founder of marketing agency OK Cool.

In a recent development, “Logos used to confer status and were a more reliable indicator of what you could afford or how you were living,” he adds. “Merch tells people what you’re into, and that’s become far more valuable. It’s a matter of signaling taste rather than wealth.”.

It has been revealed that varley points to the frenzy seen at GTA’s Selfridges launch, explaining that consumers now associate with much more than simply products, but instead entire worlds. “GTA isn’t just a game any more,” he says. “Millions of people live in it. The launch week proved it.”.

It has been revealed that whether that’s an event exclusive, an IP artefact made real for the ‘heads’, or even a staff uniform, exclusivity and experience are major drivers of hype, says Amplify’s Richardson. “Something that says, ‘I was there’, not just ‘this is what I’m into’.”.

Sources indicate that richardson also notes that fandom thrives on shared codes and signals. So his advice for brands wanting a piece of the pie? “Bringing together your own lore, something that anchors your merch in time, and the right collaborators to bring it to life in a fan-first and agile way, can turn a small run of products into a mass-reach driver.” The Rockstar Games’s GTA takeover of Miami — a reported $3.9 million deal with Miami-Dade County — sets the bar, lighting up Miami Heat’s stadium, dressing players in black-and-pink jerseys, and activating across the city.

Recent findings suggest that merch’s appeal lies in the power of the brand and what that communicates. It’s a quick win to cross categories, too. “If you build a brand that is cool, interesting, culturally relevant, aspirational, it [almost] doesn’t matter what you’re selling, because what you’re selling is the aura — this ineffable, ‘it’, cool factor,” notes Ursula founder and brand strategist Emma Hope Allwood. “Just practically, when you have these major cultural moments or rolls out like GTA, it makes sense to try to break it down into different categories — different ways for people to be part of it, rather than it just being a game.”.

Recent findings suggest that luxury brands that want to re-enter the merch market and cultural players looking to seize the growing momentum need to broach the sector carefully. “Not all merch is cool,” says Sara McAlpine, co-founder of brand and marketing studio Bikini, highlighting the recent tech brand plays. “There’s no reason to be producing a chore coat unless you’re trying to say you’re aligned with a Carhartt WIP and Japanese-denim wearing aesthetic-conscious crowd.”.

So what works? Influencer and DJ Leo Mandella visited the GTA Selfridges pop-up. He typically doesn’t consider merch cool — “[it] can look a bit gimmicky” — but the capsule delivered, he believes. “It’s very easy for gaming companies to mess up on the rest of the promo run, but Rockstar were absolutely incredible at creating a capsule of merch that was just as good as the game,” indicates Mandella, who spent £250 (roughly $329) at the pop-up. “I think merch is especially exciting when done well because you feel part of a moment. It’s not just a piece of clothing. Buying a Vice City tee or a Burger Shot uniform [the official in-game restaurant chain] makes you feel like you’re in this fictional world.”.

Inside the Selfridges GTA activation.

Sources indicate that nonetheless, for brands that still want to communicate esotericism, merch remains an astute method. Varley pinpoints the power of releasing one-off, friends-and-family T-shirts during events. He cites the Awake x Jordan T-shirts — art directed by London graffiti artist Fatzoo — given out during Notting Carnival at the Deviation stage. “That immediately orients you in a specific nucleus of that scene,” he notes. “If you weren’t there — or don’t know the individuals involved — you didn’t get one.”.

In a recent development, cut this festive galette into little squares for a hearty appetizer, or serve sizeable wedges as a vegetarian main or standout side. It’s worth seeking out savoy cabbage, the ruffly sort that looks like lace. Ordinary green cabbage, which has a higher moisture content and flatter texture, doesn’t work here (we tried).

For more Thanksgiving recipes, tips, menus, and inspiration, head to our 2026 Thanksgiving Hub.

Whisk 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt, ¼ tsp. baking powder, and 1⅔ cups (208 g) all-purpose flour in a large bowl. Add 2 oz. chilled cream cheese, cut into 1" pieces, and rub in with your fingers until incorporated (mixture will look very shaggy). Add 10 Tbsp. chilled unsalted butter, sliced ½" thick, and toss to coat in flour, then smash into smaller, flatter pieces (about chickpea size). Make a well in the center and pour in ¼ cup ice water. Toss with a fork or your hands to distribute. Knead dough in bowl just to bring together (some dry bits may remain).

In a recent development, turn dough out onto a lightly dusted surface and sprinkle with all-purpose flour. Roll out to a ½"-thick rectangle. Fold in half, rotate 90°, and fold in half again. Roll out again to a ½"-thick rectangle and repeat folding process, dusting dough with more flour as needed to prevent sticking. Pat into a ½"-thick disk and wrap tightly in plastic. Chill at least 2 hours and, preferably, up to 12 hours.

It has been revealed that do Ahead: Dough can be made 1 month ahead. Wrap disk in 2 layers of plastic and freeze instead of chilling. Thaw in refrigerator 12 hours before using.

When dough is almost done chilling, cut 1 medium head of savoy cabbage (1¾–2¼ lb.) in half and cut out triangular core at bottom; discard. Separate leaves and tear into pieces about the size of your palm. Transfer about half to a large bowl and set aside.

Melt 1 Tbsp. unsalted butter in a large skillet over medium heat. Add 1 medium white or yellow onion, thinly sliced, and season generously with kosher salt. Cook, stirring occasionally, until softened and starting to turn translucent, about 5 minutes. Add remaining 1 Tbsp. unsalted butter and ¾ tsp. cumin seeds (if using) and cook until butter is melted. Add remaining cabbage leaves and cook, stirring occasionally, until onion is translucent and lightly browned and cabbage is wilted, 18–22 minutes. Transfer to a large plate or a small baking sheet; chill in fridge or freezer until cool.

Industry observers note that place a rack in bottom third of oven; preheat to 400°. Whisk 2 garlic cloves, finely grated, ⅓ cup heavy cream, 2 Tbsp. Dijon mustard, and ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt in a measuring glass to combine. Pour cream mixture over reserved raw cabbage leaves and toss with your hands to coat. Add 5 oz. Gruyère or sharp cheddar, coarsely grated, and toss again to combine.

In a recent development, unwrap dough and roll out on a lightly floured sheet of parchment paper to a 13–14" round (some dough will extend beyond the parchment). Transfer on parchment paper to a baking sheet.

Recent findings suggest that spread cooked cabbage mixture over dough, leaving about a 1½" border around edges. Fold dough up and over filling, folding and tucking as needed to make a rustic border. Pile raw cabbage mixture on top of cooked cabbage mixture to make a dramatic heap. (It will look ridiculously high at first but will cook down when it bakes.).

It has been revealed that bake galette 25 minutes. Rotate baking sheet front to back, reduce heat to 375°, and bake until cabbage and crust are deep golden brown, 25–35 minutes. (If cabbage seems to be browning too much, reduce heat to 350° toward the end.) Let galette cool on baking sheet at least 1 hour and up to 4 hours before serving.

According to recent reports, do Ahead: Sautéed cabbage can be made 1 day ahead. Transfer to an airtight container and chill. Tightly wrap undressed raw cabbage in plastic and chill.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Listen, we all know that stuffing is the best part of Thanksgiving dinner, but because of the butter, eggs, and chicken broth that usually go into classic stuffing, it's a dish that vegans can't always enjoy—until now! We created a stuffing that's so delicious, you might even be convinced to make a few of your other holiday classics into vegan Thanksgiving versions.

Start your stuffing off by preheating the oven to 200° and slicing the bread into roughly 1” cubes. Spread the cubes in a single layer on a large baking sheet and bake for about 20 minutes, until the bread is nice and crisp.

Remove the bread from the oven and turn the temperature up to 350°. Grease a 13” x 9” baking dish with cooking spray and heat oil in a large skillet over medium heat. Add onion to the skillet and cook for about 5 minutes until lightly charred in some spots, then add the celery and garlic and continue to cook, stirring occasionally, until the celery starts to turn translucent. Pour in the vegetable stock and scrape up any browned bits—this is where all the flavor is. Season with salt and pepper.

Mix the bread cubes and chopped herbs in the vegetable stock mixture until well combined, then transfer to the prepared baking dish.

Sources indicate that cover the dish tightly with aluminum foil and place it in the oven to bake for 40 minutes. Carefully remove the foil and continue baking for another 35 minutes, until the stuffing is golden brown and crisp on top.

The full list of ingredients and instructions can be found in the recipe below.

It has been revealed that looking for more vegan holiday inspo? Whip up our cauliflower stuffing for a low-carb option, or try out our vegetarian mushroom gravy or vegan mashed potatoes to truly complete your spread!

Any leftovers can be stored in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 4 days. You can also prepare this dish ahead of time, as it’s the kind of dish that we think tastes even better after sitting for a day.

It has been revealed that in the midst of a rich meal, something fresh and acidic keeps your taste buds awake. Where lettuce splashed with vinaigrette can feel like an afterthought, a juicy, savory-slanting pear salad is worth making room for on a plate full of turkey and cornbread. This is the antithesis of the haphazardly chunked together fruit salads you find at the supermarket for a brunch or dessert spread. Keep the focus on crisp-tart pears—apples also work—and it’s a welcome accompaniment to the other hearty dishes. Sliced razor-thin (use a mandoline) and fanned out on a platter, the fruit acts as an edible canvas for wisps of cheese and clusters of honey-roasted seeds. Leftovers (if you have any, of course) are delightful spooned over a well-toasted and buttered slice of multigrain bread the next day.

In a recent development, pick firm green pears (Bartlett and Anjou are fair game; use Asian pears in a pinch) to ensure they hold their shape once sliced—even a little underripe is better than slightly over. After slicing, have a taste: If they are very tart, add 1 tsp. honey to the dressing; if fairly sweet, skip it.

For more Thanksgiving recipes, tips, menus, and inspiration, head to our 2026 Thanksgiving Hub.

Preheat oven to 325°. Whisk 3 Tbsp. honey, 1 tsp. garlic powder, ½ tsp. freshly ground pepper, 3 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil, and ¾ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt in a large bowl to combine. Add 1 cup raw sunflower seeds, pumpkin seeds (pepitas), and/or coarsely crushed raw nuts (such as walnuts, almonds, and/or hazelnuts) and stir to coat. Spread out in a single layer on a parchment-lined rimmed baking sheet; reserve bowl.

Sources indicate that bake seed mixture until golden brown, 12–14 minutes. (Honey mixture will puff up a bit but will deflate when you stir.) Toss honey-roasted seeds, then let cool. Toss again just to break up.

It has been revealed that whisk 3 Tbsp. fresh lemon juice, 1 tsp. Dijon mustard, a pinch of kosher salt, and remaining 1 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in reserved bowl. Add 2 lb. firm green pears (such as Bartlett and/or Anjou; about 4 large), cored, thinly sliced, to dressing and gently toss to coat.

It has been revealed that arrange pears on a large flat platter. Scatter honey-roasted seeds over and top with 2 oz. Parmesan, aged white cheddar, or Manchego cheese, shaved.

According to recent reports, do Ahead: Honey-roasted seeds can be made 6 hours ahead. Store at room temperature.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

These maple-glazed carrots don’t hold back on the butter—or the brown sugar. Roasted with pure maple syrup and crushed red pepper flakes, they turn tender and glossy with a sweet-hot kick that complements everything from ham to lamb to green bean casserole.

Recent findings suggest that the recipe began with Barbie—not the doll, but Andy Baraghani’s cousin’s former girlfriend. Her syrupy-sweet carrots became a fixture at family Christmas dinners. Some dishes are meant to last; some relationships aren’t.

Industry observers note that for BA’s version, Andy traded the original’s hours-long cooking time for a hotter roast that gives the carrots browned edges and a buttery glaze. There’s no separate sauce to simmer: Everything goes straight onto a foil-lined (for easier cleanup) rimmed baking sheet, with regular tossing to coat the carrots in syrup as they cook. Finish with flaky salt for crunch and a welcome contrast to the sweetness.

Recent findings suggest that no. This recipe calls for scrubbed, unpeeled carrots—give them a thorough cleaning and leave the skins on.

How do I keep the glaze from burning?

According to recent reports, keep the carrot pieces similar in thickness, halving or quartering larger ones lengthwise. Check the glaze each time you toss the carrots, especially once the edges begin browning: The sugars can darken swiftly. Use tenderness and browned edges as your guide rather than waiting out the clock if the carrots are already done.

For a more savory version, try our Easy Roasted Carrots.

According to recent reports, place rack in middle of oven and preheat oven to 400°. Line a rimmed baking sheet with 3 sheets of foil (you’ll need it!). Cut 2 lb. medium carrots, tops trimmed to about ½", scrubbed, on a diagonal into 3" pieces (halved or quartered lengthwise if large).

Spread out carrots on foil. Evenly top with 6 Tbsp. unsalted butter, cut into pieces, ⅓ cup (packed; 70 g) light brown sugar, ⅓ cup pure maple syrup, and ¾ tsp. crushed red pepper flakes. Season with kosher salt and toss to combine.

Industry observers note that roast carrots, tossing every 20 minutes, until tender and browned around the edges, 50–60 minutes. Watch closely as the carrots begin to brown; the glaze can darken quickly. Transfer to a platter and drizzle with any remaining syrup. Sprinkle with flaky sea salt (if using).

Recent findings suggest that for those who might shudder at the thought of eating raw hardy greens like collards or kale, this vibrant side inspired by the French bistro classic leeks vinaigrette is the answer. Simmered past squeaky-raw yet well short of meltingly braised, they offer substantial bite, like al dente pasta. The mustard dressing couldn’t be simpler to make—use it as a base for any salad you might serve this season. It’s punchy enough to stand up to winter vegetables or any sturdy bitter green.

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 325°. Toast ½ cup raw walnuts on a rimmed baking sheet, tossing halfway through, until golden brown, 10–12 minutes.

It has been revealed that meanwhile, cook 2 bunches collard greens, ribs and stems removed, leaves cut into 2" pieces, in a large pot of generously salted boiling water until just tender, 9–11 minutes. Using tongs, immediately transfer to a large bowl of ice water and let cool.

Whisk 2 garlic cloves, finely grated, ¼ cup white wine vinegar, 2 Tbsp. Dijon mustard, preferably country-style, ⅓ cup extra-virgin olive oil, ¼ cup (packed) coarsely chopped tarragon, 2 tsp. sugar, and 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt in a medium bowl to combine. Set dressing aside.

Recent findings suggest that transfer toasted walnuts to a small bowl and drizzle with remaining 1 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil. Sprinkle with a generous pinch each of sugar and salt and toss to coat. Taste and add more sugar if needed (nuts should be more sweet than salty). Set seasoned walnuts aside.

Recent findings suggest that drain collard greens and squeeze gently to remove excess water. Transfer to bowl with reserved dressing and toss to coat evenly. Cover and chill at least 15 minutes and up to 2 hours.

Arrange greens in a shallow bowl or on a platter and spoon any dressing remaining in bowl over. Top with seasoned walnuts and tarragon leaves.

In a recent development, do Ahead: Walnuts can be toasted and dressing can be made 1 day ahead. Store walnuts airtight at room temperature. Cover dressing and chill.
